title: Give Every Medical or Dental Practice System a Recovery Owner
summary: Assign a primary and backup person to coordinate recovery for each critical practice system, then test one recovery path today.
body: Independent medical and dental practices depend on several connected systems to keep a normal day moving: clinical records, imaging, scheduling, phones, email, payments, internet service, and the network underneath them. A vendor may operate the software or store the backup, but the practice still needs someone who knows what to do when that system is unavailable. The useful question is not simply, ‘Do we have a backup?’ It is, ‘Who owns the recovery process, and how will that person know it worked?’

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services says in its Security Rule summary, last reviewed August 7, 2026, that regulated organizations need contingency procedures for emergencies that damage systems containing electronic protected health information. Those procedures include backing up information, restoring lost data, and continuing critical business processes in emergency mode. HHS also notes that cloud-service agreements can address availability, backup, recovery, and security responsibilities. A cloud subscription can support recovery, but it does not assign your staff, make the vendor call, or decide when the practice should use a manual workflow.

Today’s owner checklist is short: list each critical system; name a primary recovery owner and a backup owner; record the vendor or support contact; identify where approved credentials and instructions are stored; note the last successful restore or recovery test; and write the temporary workflow staff should use while the system is down. The practice owner or office manager should maintain the list, while the people who actually run each workflow should confirm that the instructions match daily operations.

Start with one decision question for every system: what must be available first for safe, orderly work to resume? Then ask who can authorize emergency access, who can reach the vendor after hours, how staff will learn that the system is unavailable, and who will confirm that recovered information is complete before normal work resumes. For a dental imaging system, the answer may differ from scheduling or email. Treat each system according to its role instead of giving every outage the same response.

Do not place passwords, patient details, or full recovery instructions on an open contact sheet. The checklist should point authorized staff to the protected location where that information is kept. It should also distinguish a vendor’s responsibility from the practice’s responsibility. If the vendor restores its service but a local scanner, network connection, or workstation still cannot reach it, the practice needs a named person to coordinate the remaining steps rather than assuming the ticket is finished.

A full disaster exercise is not required to improve this today. Choose the system that would disrupt the most appointments, verify both owners, confirm the support path, and walk through the first ten minutes of an outage without using real patient information. Record what is missing and set a date to test the next system. Calm recovery starts with clear ownership, current contacts, and one practiced step at a time.
